CHIEF COMPLAINT
Worsening headaches over the past few months with newly diagnosed pituitary lesion.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
This is a 52-year-old male presenting in neurosurgical consultation at the request of Dr. Henry Howard for evaluation of a pituitary lesion incidentally discovered during workup for headaches. Patient initially presented to his primary care provider on 3/1/21 complaining of worsening headaches over the past few months. He denies any significant trouble with headaches in the past. Brain MRI and serology were initiated as workup, which revealed the pituitary lesion. The headaches began approximately 3 months ago and have been gradually worsening. Initial severity was 3 out of 10, now approximately 6 out of 10. Headaches are located behind the eyes, described as a dull nagging ache, worse in the morning, lasting a few hours at a time. Nothing makes them better or worse. Patient denies associated nausea, fever, rash, neck stiffness, numbness, tingling, or syncope. He reports recently bumping into door frames. Patient has not noticed change in vision, though eyes were checked in the fall. He tried acetaminophen a few times without relief and discontinued it.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies fever, rash, neck stiffness, nausea, numbness, tingling, or syncope. Denies recent vision changes. Reports recent episodes of bumping into door frames. Otherwise unremarkable.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Unremarkable.

MEDICATIONS
No current medications. Patient tried acetaminophen for headaches without benefit.

ALLERGIES
Not documented.

FAMILY HISTORY
Patient was adopted and has no knowledge of family medical history.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient works as a computer programmer. He is married for 25 years and recently purchased a home. He denies alcohol use, tobacco use, and recreational drug use. He has never used any of these substances.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Patient is alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Affect is appropriate and speech is fluent. Cranial nerve examination is grossly intact. No focal motor or sensory deficit in upper or lower extremities. Visual acuity and eye movements are normal. Pupils are equal and reactive. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. Color vision is normal.

RESULTS
Labs dated 3/3/21 reviewed including CBC, electrolytes, coagulation studies, and CRP, all normal. Pituitary hormone profile demonstrates low TSH, all other results normal. Brain MRI with contrast from 3/4/21 reveals a well-defined pituitary lesion with elevation and compression of the optic chiasm. Ventricles are normal in size with no other abnormalities noted.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Pituitary adenoma with optic chiasmal compression. Patient is symptomatic with clinical and radiographical evidence of optic chiasmal compression causing bitemporal hemianopia and progressive headaches. Benign-appearing lesion, though pathologic confirmation will be obtained from resected specimen. Surgical intervention indicated. Plan for transsphenoidal approach for resection and decompression of pituitary fossa. Discussed surgical risks including anesthesia-related complications (myocardial infarction, stroke, death), operative risks (infection, CSF leak, meningitis, seizure, stroke, permanent neurologic deficit, death, need for further surgery). Preoperative visual field testing to be arranged for baseline comparison. Patient to see surgery scheduler to establish operative timeline. Ophthalmology referral placed for full examination and formal visual field testing prior to surgery.
